name: Peter the Great
info: Peter I (1672–1725), known as the Great, was tsar of all Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721, remembered for the Great Northern War, the founding of Saint Petersburg and sweeping Westernizing reforms.

facts.born: 9 June 1672; son of Tsar Alexei Mikailovich and his second wife Natalya Naryshkina, of the Romanov dynasty
facts.died: 8 February 1725, between four and five in the morning, of an illness of the bladder found at autopsy to be gangrenous; buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral
facts.role: Tsar of all Russia, 1682–1721 (jointly with Ivan V until 1696); Emperor of All Russia, 1721–1725
facts.known: The Great Northern War and the victory at Poltava; founding Saint Petersburg; the Russian Navy; the Grand Embassy to Western Europe; the Governing Senate, the collegia and the Table of Ranks; the Holy Synod in place of the patriarchate

t: Peter I reigned from 1682 to 1725, sole ruler from 1696, and in 1721 took the title Emperor of All Russia after victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War.

He founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and made it the capital, built a navy, and reorganised the state through the Governing Senate, the collegia, the Table of Ranks and a Holy Synod that replaced the patriarchate.

His reforms were imposed by force: he crushed revolts such as the Streltsy and Bulavin rebellions, and historians still argue whether he set Russia on a modern course or, as Evgeny Anisimov put it, created an administrative command system.
dyk: Boyars who wished to keep their beards after Peter's return from Western Europe had to pay an annual beard tax of one hundred rubles.

sections.early:
Peter I was born on 9 June 1672, the son of Tsar Alexei Mikailovich and his second wife, Natalya Naryshkina. He grew up at the Izmaylovo estate and was taught from an early age by tutors his father engaged, most notably Nikita Zotov, Patrick Gordon and Paul Menesius. When Alexei died in 1676 the throne passed to Peter's elder half-brother, the crippled Feodor III, while government was largely run by Artamon Matveyev, head of the Naryshkin family and one of Peter's chief childhood protectors.

From 1682 to 1689 Peter and his mother lived at Preobrazhenskoye, away from power. At sixteen he found an old English boat on the estate, had it restored and learned to sail. In the German Quarter of Moscow he sought out foreign experts: Andrew Vinius taught him Dutch, and the Dutch carpenters Frans Timmerman and Karsten Brandt helped him. He studied arithmetic, geometry and fortification, built ships at Pereslavl-Zalessky, sailed on Lake Pleshcheyevo and drilled a toy army in mock battles. He grew extremely tall, reportedly 6 ft 8 in (2.03 m), and had noticeable facial tics. In 1689 his mother arranged his marriage to Eudoxia Lopukhina, which proved a failure.
sections.rise:
When Feodor III died childless in 1682, the families of Alexei's two wives, the Miloslavskys and the Naryshkins, fought over the succession. The Boyar Duma chose the ten-year-old Peter, with his mother as regent, but in April and May 1682 his half-sister Sophia led a rebellion of the streltsy, the elite military corps, in which some of Peter's relatives and friends, among them Matveyev, were murdered, and Peter witnessed some of the violence. Peter and his half-brother Ivan V were then proclaimed joint tsars, Ivan as senior, and Sophia ruled as regent for seven years.

By the summer of 1689, with Sophia weakened by two failed campaigns against the Crimean Khanate, Peter planned to take power. Warned that she was conspiring with streltsy leaders, he fled by night to the Troitse-Sergiyeva Lavra, where supporters gathered to him. Sophia was overthrown and forced into a convent. Even so, power was exercised by his mother until her death in 1694; Ivan V remained a formal co-ruler, and Peter became sole ruler when Ivan died in 1696.
sections.deeds:
Seeking outlets to the sea, Peter attacked the Ottoman fortress of Azov in 1695 without success, then built a navy at Voronezh and took Azov in July 1696. In March 1697 he left on the 18-month Grand Embassy, travelling under a false name; he worked in a Dutch East India Company shipyard in Amsterdam, studied at Deptford and the Royal Mint in England, and hired many foreign craftsmen. He failed, however, to widen the alliance against the Ottomans. Back home he ordered courtiers into European dress and introduced the Julian calendar from 1700. In the Great Northern War against Sweden he was defeated at Narva in 1700, rebuilt his army, founded Saint Petersburg on 29 June 1703 and in 1709 decisively defeated Charles XII at Poltava. The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia Ingria, Estonia, Livonia and much of Karelia.

At home he created the Governing Senate in 1711, divided Russia into eight governorates, set up collegia in place of the old agencies after 1718 and issued the Table of Ranks in 1722, ranking nobles by service rather than birth. He moved the capital to Saint Petersburg in 1712, replaced the patriarchate with a Holy Synod in 1721, founded schools of mathematics, navigation and engineering, introduced the civil script, promoted mining and industry, and replaced the land and household taxes with a poll tax.
sections.opponents:
Peter's reforms met resistance that he suppressed brutally, including the risings of the Streltsy, the Bashkirs and Astrakhan, and the Bulavin Rebellion, the greatest civil uprising of his reign. After the second Streltsy revolt of 1698, 4,600 rebels were imprisoned and around 1,182 tortured and executed, their bodies displayed as a warning; the corps was disbanded. Boyars and Old Believers resented the beard decree, and to Old Believers he was the Antichrist for his calendar and poll tax. The new poll tax fell on serfs and paupers, and from 1721 factory owners of any rank could buy serfs. In 1721 he had Matwei Gagarin, governor of Siberia, executed.

His own family suffered too. His son Alexei, suspected of plotting against him, was tried by a secular court, confessed under torture and was sentenced to death; locked up in 1718, he died in prison, most likely of his injuries. Alexei's mother Eudoxia was tried on false charges of adultery, publicly flogged and confined. In war Peter's Pruth campaign against the Ottomans was a disaster, and the Ottomans called him "Mad Peter" for his willingness to sacrifice large numbers of troops; an expedition against Khiva in 1717 ended with the whole force slaughtered.
sections.last:
In his last years Peter continued to reform. On 2 November 1721 he was proclaimed Emperor of All Russia, a title recognised by Poland, Prussia and Sweden but not by the other European monarchs. In 1722 his decree on the succession abolished the custom of passing the throne to direct male descendants, and the same year he launched the Russo-Persian War of 1722–1723, which won Derbent, Baku, Gilan and other provinces; within twelve years all were handed back to Persia. In 1724 he had his second wife, Catherine, crowned empress.

From the winter of 1723 Peter suffered from problems of the bladder and urinary tract, and in the summer of 1724 doctors operated on him. According to a legend recorded only by the chronicler Jacob von Staehlin, and doubted by some historians, he made his illness worse that November by wading into icy water at Lakhta to rescue drowning soldiers. In January 1725 he fell ill again with uremia; legend says he wrote an unfinished note, "Leave all to ...". He died early on 8 February 1725, and an autopsy found his bladder infected with gangrene. He was buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral.
sections.legacy:
Peter is credited with turning Russia rapidly into a major European power, and many institutions of the Russian state trace their origins to his reign; the Table of Ranks lasted until the monarchy fell in 1917, and Saint Petersburg remained the capital until 1918. The Russian Academy of Sciences was founded in 1724, and some 3,500 words from western languages entered Russian in his time. James Cracraft calls the Petrine revolution essentially a cultural revolution, seen in Petrine Baroque architecture, dress and naturalistic portraiture.

His legacy has always divided Russians. The historian Riasanovsky points to images in black and white: God or Antichrist, architect of Russia's greatness or destroyer of national culture. Voltaire's 1759 biography made him a man of the Enlightenment and Pushkin's The Bronze Horseman a romantic creator, while the Slavophiles deplored his Westernization. Stalin admired how he strengthened the state, and Soviet historians stressed both his achievements and the oppression of the common people. Historian Y. Vodarsky argued in 1993 that he held Russia back for a century and a half, and Evgeny Anisimov called him "the true ancestor of Stalin".

summary: Peter I ruled Russia from 1682, alone from 1696, and became its first emperor in 1721 after defeating Sweden in the Great Northern War. He founded Saint Petersburg, built a navy and remade the state, the church and the nobility's ranks, suppressing revolts harshly; he died in 1725, and his legacy is still disputed.
